author: RichardMCNgo
text: What do I mean by pattern? In general, a structure which can be recognised by some computable algorithm. For our purposes: a structure which can be recognised/understood by the human algorithm (or similar algorithms, e.g. AGIs which understand our universe).

author: RichardMCNgo
text: To be more specific: concepts are patterns which arise in minds, and minds are a type of computable algorithm, and computable algorithms are equivalent to Turing Machines, and Turing Machines are a mathematical construction. (And maths in turn is grounded in logic, e.g. via ZFC.)

author: RichardMCNgo
text: We inhabit a physical universe of objects and forces and an abstract universe of ideas and thoughts. Physics showed that the former consists of high-level patterns of quarks, etc. Turing showed that the latter consists of high-level patterns in math: an equally crucial reduction.

author: RichardMCNgo
text:
4 premises:
1. We’ll build AIs which are much more intelligent than humans.
2. Those AIs will be autonomous agents which pursue large-scale goals.
3. Those goals will be misaligned with ours.
4. The development of such AIs would lead to them gaining control of humanity’s future.

author: RichardMCNgo
text: The core claim: human intelligence allows us to build complex societies and advanced technology to control the world. But AIs will eventually become more capable than us at these types of tasks. If they don’t want to obey us, then humanity might lose control over its future.

author: RichardMCNgo

author: RichardMCNgo
text: Or consider the continuum between a physicist talking about special relativity, vs a layperson who can't distinguish it from general relativity, vs someone who can't distinguish it from Newton's laws, vs a child saying those words without knowing what a scientific theory is.

text: By accepting continuity of reference, you can make rigid designators less rigid. "A version of Aristotle who died young" refers. "A version of Aristotle born in the year 2000" refers much less. "A version of Aristotle born in 2000 with the same genes as me" barely refers at all.

author: RichardMCNgo
text: One must always crop and contort the world to squeeze it into a human-comprehemsible conceptual framework. The question is always merely: how much is lost in the process? Or (to use a CS term that really should become more common): how leaky are our abstractions?

text: Lastly, decentralisation makes it unusually misleading to judge movements by headline examples, because it's so hard to tell who endorses them. To think clearly on these issues, we must internalise that social media polarises not just the outgroup, but you and I.

author: RichardMCNgo
text: This all means we should be very careful in pattern-matching current social movements to historical examples (for good or ill). Their decentralisation makes them stronger but less coherent; it makes examples of their misbehavior more salient and more common but less important.

author: RichardMCNgo
text: Does this leave a power vacuum? Yes, but it's not easily fillable. Within feminism the influence of aggressive men is constrained. Meanwhile the public faces of climate and animal advocacy are children and celebrities: it's hard to build a power bloc of future people and animals.

author: RichardMCNgo
text: Meanwhile the fringes push radical ideas without anyone to rein them in. But they also lack any central authority as backup. The Twitter firehose provides reinforcements, but that's fickle and short-lived. So there's less long-term pressure, and very little organised violence.

author: RichardMCNgo
text: You also get more idealistic movements, since the loudest voices don't have to struggle to implement policies in messy reality. Indeed, there are no consistently loudest voices - rather, what's broadcast is a tapestry of thousands of "15 minutes of fame".

author: RichardMCNgo
text: Of course these movements draw on existing scholarship, but they are less able to translate it from specialist terminology to authoritative public-facing manifestos. This also limits the extent to which opponents can push back by directly critiquing the core concepts.

author: RichardMCNgo
text: In exchange, they have much less legibility and message discipline. It's far less clear what they stand for, their core tenets, or what their terminology even means. Lately you see this with "defund the police" crowdsourcing definitions in realtime. https://t.co/z0OQ3SysUE

quoted.text: Mottes and baileys are probably the most important concept you need to understand online political interactions.

author: RichardMCNgo
text: You also protect against cooption by elites, and cults of personality. Preventing this becomes harder as movements amass more power (e.g. see almost any revolution) but so far it's remarkable how little any individual currently gets to set the agenda, or is immune to criticism.

author: RichardMCNgo

There are positive and negative effects. On one hand, you have automatic grassroots mobilisation, and higher political engagement in an era of declining voter turnout. You can see the efficacy in the sheer speed of public opinion shift on gay marriage.

author: RichardMCNgo
text: The open question is where these insights will come from. Academia: a digital Peterson or Zizek? Science fiction: Gibson updated? Hacker culture? Or just a citizen of the internet? I'd bet on the last - but so far the most insightful internet thinkers have gazed outward.

author: RichardMCNgo
text: That requires brilliance, precisely because the internet is such an all-encompassing ocean. For those on the shore it's hard to understand the currents; for those submerged, it's hard to see the one vast whole. To change how the internet generations see themselves will take both.

text: Innovism favours mistake theory over conflict theory. It's anti-credentialism. It cares about exponential growth and the big picture. It emphasises how much the material state of humanity has improved. Innovism is driven by definite optimism. Innovism thinks it's time to build.

author: RichardMCNgo
